response.text:
Good — here are concrete, decision-friendly layout changes (with why each helps). I’ve grouped them so you can pick which trade-offs you prefer before we render.

Overall structure & visual flow
- Change: Move from a strict “stacked photos left / headline across top / QR bottom-right” to a subtle two-column grid (photos in a left column ~30–40% width, headline + copy + CTA in the right column).
  - Why: creates clear reading flow (left-to-right) and balances visual weight so the headline and CTA don’t compete with the photos. Keeps the photos prominent but gives text breathing room.

Headline treatment
- Change: Break the headline into 1–2 lines and left-align it in the right column rather than centering across the whole top.
  - Why: left alignment ties the headline visually to the photos and improves scanability. Two-line headlines are easier to read at a glance than one long centered line.
- Change: Increase contrast and size of the headline; use a strong weight for the key word(s) and lighter weight for the rest (or a different color accent).
  - Why: establishes hierarchy so viewers immediately know the message.

Photos and imagery
- Change: Make the two photos visually unified (same crop, lighting treatment, and color treatment — e.g., warm duotone or desaturated with a color accent) and treat them as a single unit (touching/overlapping slightly or framed together).
  - Why: prevents the left column from feeling like two separate posters; creates a cohesive hero area and strengthens brand identity.
- Change: Add a thin vertical divider or color accent between the photo column and the text column.
  - Why: gives structure and helps guide the eye from imagery to the headline/CTA.

CTA and QR code
- Change: Move the QR slightly inward from the extreme bottom-right and place a short CTA label directly above/left of it (e.g., “Scan to apply” or “Start here →”).
  - Why: QR at the very edge can get lost or be harder to scan; adding a CTA clarifies the action and increases conversions.
- Change: Ensure a clear quiet zone (padding) around the QR and increase its visual prominence with a subtle outline or light halo if the background is very dark.
  - Why: improves scanability and makes it obvious that the code is actionable.

Secondary copy and microcopy
- Change: Add a one-line subhead under the headline or a 2–3 word benefit near the QR (e.g., “No experience needed” / “Apply in 60s”).
  - Why: answers viewer questions fast and gives incentive to scan the QR.

Contrast, color, and legibility
- Change: For a dark background, use high-contrast text (white or very light neutrals) and reserve brand/accent color for highlights (CTA, key words, divider).
  - Why: improves legibility from a distance and keeps the design clean.
- Change: Ensure any photo overlays or tints still leave faces and key details readable (avoid heavy black overlays over faces).
  - Why: faces draw attention — preserve them so the viewer connects emotionally.

Balance & spacing
- Change: Increase outer margins and white space around the headline and QR; compress the stacked photos slightly if they feel too dominant.
  - Why: breathing room improves clarity and prevents the layout from feeling cramped or top-heavy.
- Change: Align baseline grid so headline, subhead, and CTA line up visually — consistent left edge for text blocks.
  - Why: cleaner, more professional look and faster reading.

Accessibility & practical checks
- Change: For print or large-format posters, verify QR physical size and quiet zone; for digital, ensure QR resolution and safe tappable area.
  - Why: makes sure the QR actually works in the final medium.
- Change: Include a short URL or short code near the QR as a fallback.
  - Why: provides an alternative for people who can’t scan.

Optional stylistic variations (pick one)
- Option A (Modern/direct): Tight grid, bold headline, monochrome photos with one accent color — very readable and conversion-oriented.
- Option B (Human/warm): Larger faces, warmer photo duotone, rounded CTA button near QR — friendlier, more aspirational.
- Option C (Dynamic/edgy): Slight photo overlap, angled divider, headline partially overlaying photos — eye-catching but riskier for legibility.

Quick questions before we render
1. Is this poster for print (what final size) or digital/screen? (affects QR size and font sizes)
2. Do you have brand colors and typefaces we must stick to, or are those flexible?
3. Which stylistic option above do you prefer (A, B, or C), or do you want a hybrid?

Tell me those details and which suggestions you want to adopt; I’ll incorporate them into the render instructions.
